title: Why Not Burn Him With a Look?
hookLine: the gods ask why the goddess didn't burn Mahisha with a glance, and find mercy in her sword
carry: the goddess is kind even to her enemies
tomorrow: two demon brothers take heaven. who do the gods remember?

cards: If the goddess could end Mahisha with a single look, why fight at all? The gods themselves ask it. In the fourth chapter the buffalo is dead.

The gods, Indra at their head, bow with necks bent and bodies thrilled, and praise her. Partway through their hymn they wonder out loud: you could have burned him to ash just by looking. Why didn't you?
Their own answer is stranger. Today, the hymn, and the promise she leaves before she vanishes.

teach.h: FORTUNE IN THE HOMES OF THE GOOD.
teach.b: The hymn begins wide. In paraphrase, the gods bow to the goddess who spread out the whole world by her own power, whom even Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma can't fully describe. Then it comes into ordinary houses.

She is good fortune in the homes of those who do good, and misfortune in the homes of those who do harm; understanding in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, modesty in people of noble birth.
In this hymn she isn't only on a battlefield. She's at the kitchen table, in what a house becomes. Then the question, and the gods answer it themselves.
In paraphrase: so that the demons, purified by your weapons, might reach the higher worlds. Even toward enemies, your thought is kind.
These demons had done enough harm to deserve a long time in hell, and you killed them in battle so they might reach heaven instead. In the gods' own hymn, the sword is a kind of mercy.
Hindu stories say it again and again: an enemy who falls at the hand of the divine is set free, not thrown away. Then the goddess tells them to choose a boon.
They say, in paraphrase: our enemy is dead, so everything is done.

teach.h: WHY NOT BURN HIM WITH A LOOK?
teach.b: But if we remember you again, come and end our worst troubles, and may whoever praises you with this hymn prosper.

teach.h: REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.
teach.b: That promise is why many Hindus recite this text, or its verses, when trouble comes: remembered, she comes.

teach.h: THE SWORD AS A KIND OF MERCY.
teach.b: The next chapter opens with new demons, and the gods, cornered again, remembering exactly this.

how: The gods' hymn in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, sometimes called the Shakradi Stuti after Indra (Shakra), is recited as part of the whole text and is also chanted on its own by some devotees of the goddess.

o: a curse spoken over the demons before a war
the goddess's glory, a text of hymns and battles
a list of boons that the gods ask from Shiva

games.q: the gods' hymn — tap the pairs.
p: in the homes of the good
in the hearts of the learned
so even enemies might reach higher worlds
come when we remember you in trouble

s: the hymn says the goddess wants her enemies destroyed for good
her thought is kind even toward enemies: slain by her weapons, the demons reach the higher worlds.
the gods ask why she didn't burn Mahisha with a look
and answer it themselves: so that, purified by her weapons, even enemies might reach the higher worlds.
after the hymn, the goddess stays with the gods
she grants their boon and vanishes.

games.q: you're the gods. the goddess has killed your enemy and offers you a boon. what do you ask for?
o: that she stay and rule heaven.
that she come and end our troubles whenever we remember her.
games.why: they say everything is done, then ask: when we remember you again, come and end our worst troubles. she agrees, and vanishes.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has made life harder for you, not the hardest, just someone, and breathe with whatever rises.
Then, without excusing anything they did, let one small wish form for their good, that they find some peace; you don't have to mean it completely.
If you pray, hold them before God or the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let the wish ride out on the breath.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the gods' hymn: kindness even toward enemies, and a promise to come when remembered.

orig.note: Sanskrit: stuti, a hymn of praise. The fourth chapter is the gods' stuti to the goddess.

carryVoice: Your line: the goddess is kind even to her enemies. Even her sword, the hymn says, is mercy. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 4 (the gods' hymn and the boon)
